title: Self-Assessment: Paul Graham on Three Traits of Great Teachers
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: Dave uses an essay by Paul Graham, answering an offbeat question about what made his best teachers good, as a self-assessment tool for teachers, mapping Graham's three traits (high standards, liking students, being genuinely interested in the subject) onto his own Five Key Beliefs framework of Credibility, Value, and Belonging. For each trait he unpacks the underlying psychology, citing the "magic feedback" research on high-expectations messaging boosting revision follow-through — especially for underrepresented students — and shares a personal story about learning to love teaching Fahrenheit 451 despite his own reservations about the book, modeling how disinterest can be converted into contagious enthusiasm.
points: Reframes Paul Graham's three traits of great teachers (high standards, liking students, interest in the subject) as levers on Credibility, Value, and Belonging, connecting an outsider's offhand answer to his own established motivation framework.

Cites "magic feedback" research showing that prefacing critical feedback with a high-expectations message significantly increased revision follow-through, especially among underrepresented students, as evidence that high standards signal care rather than harshness.

Argues that "liking students" is a skill that takes deliberate work, not an innate trait some teachers have and others don't, listing concrete practices (prayer, reflection, forcing a smile, focusing on the good) for building it.

Shares a personal, self-deprecating example, disliking teaching Fahrenheit 451 until he reframed the unit as an open argument with students about the text's flaws, to model how enthusiasm can be built by going "right straight through" the thing you don't enjoy.
quotes: The best teachers I remember from school, had three things in common.
Like three year olds testing their parents, students will test teachers to see if they can get away with low-quality work or bad behavior. They won't respect the teachers who don't call them on it.
Like dogs, kids can tell very accurately whether or not someone wishes them well. I think a lot of our teachers either never liked kids much, or got burned out and started not to like them.
It's hard, ya'll. And figuring out how to like all kinds of people is literally one of the most personally profound things that this job can give you.
My point is — the way to enthusiasm, sometimes, is right straight through the thing that makes you unenthusiastic.

Study participants who received that message with their feedback were significantly more likely to apply feedback to future drafts and submit better quality essays — especially African American students who were under-represented at the school being studied.
